faqs.q: What is living in my Jacksonville chimney?
faqs.a: Most often a raccoon — mother raccoons favor chimneys as den sites in spring, and a chattering, thumping flue is the classic sign — but chimney swifts, a protected migratory bird, also nest in Jacksonville flues in summer and may not be disturbed while active. We inspect with a camera before recommending anything: a raccoon family gets a humane eviction timed to the young, a cap goes on after, and a swift nest means waiting until fall migration, then capping. Diagnosis first is the whole ballgame with chimneys.

Jacksonville.wildlife_intro:
Jacksonville is the largest city by land in the continental United States, and its wildlife map is just as sprawling: historic Riverside and Springfield porches, Southside subdivisions, the Beaches corridor, Mandarin's oak hammocks along the St. Johns, and rural Northside acreage. Gray squirrels and raccoons own the older attics; roof rats work the river neighborhoods; armadillos dig everywhere the soil is sandy; and along the Trout River and the marsh creeks, otters, wading birds, and marsh rabbits remind everyone how much wild ground the city still contains.

Neighborhood age predicts our Jacksonville inspection list. Pre-war homes need chimney caps and eave carpentry; 1970s Southside ranches need soffit and vent work; new Northside and Nocatee-edge builds need builder-gap sealing. Bats — evening bats are common here, and big browns occur this far north — are excluded only in the August 15 to April 15 window. One number reaches us across the whole city: (844) 544-3498.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Jacksonville Beach?
faqs.a: Jax Beach quotes are built on corrosion math: marine-grade exclusion costs more upfront and half as much over five years, and we show both options in writing. Raised-home skirt work is priced by the opening and footage after inspection, combined with attic sealing into one figure.

faqs.q: Animals keep getting under my raised Jacksonville Beach house — how do you stop it?
faqs.a: By treating the under-house as a room that needs a door policy. We identify who is using it — opossums and skunks are the usual tenants, raccoons the destructive ones — fit one-way exits or trap at the active entrances, confirm it is empty, then install buried-edge, corrosion-resistant skirting all the way around. Leaving one gap for 'ventilation' restarts the tenancy; real vents get screened vents, not openings. The result is a crawl space that stays animal-free in a neighborhood where the pressure never stops.

Jacksonville Beach.wildlife_intro:
Jacksonville Beach is dense barrier-island living — beach cottages, mid-rise condos, and rebuilt waterfront homes between the ocean and the Intracoastal. Salt, sand, and small lots shape the work: roof rats in the palms and beachside attics, raccoons under raised houses and in dumpsters behind the beach boulevard businesses, opossums in crawl spaces, and shorebirds — protected, all of them — nesting in the dunes each spring. Sea turtle season lighting rules remind everyone how regulated this shoreline is.

Beachside exclusion has to survive the environment: stainless and marine-grade materials, because standard screening rusts out in a few seasons this close to the surf. Raised-house crawl spaces are the island's signature job — skirt them properly and the opossum and skunk traffic under the house ends. For condo associations we work building by building, documenting entries floor by floor so boards can budget the sealing as a capital item.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Atlantic Beach attic always a removal job?
faqs.a: Our squirrel work is for the eastern gray squirrel only — it is the attic species here. Fox squirrels may not be taken or pursued in Florida, and a large, slow squirrel on the ground is an identification stop, not a booking, especially in southwest Florida where the Big Cypress fox squirrel is State Threatened. For gray squirrels, our crew uses one-way exclusion and seals the roofline so the animals leave and cannot return.

Atlantic Beach.wildlife_intro:
In Atlantic Beach, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — Florida's largest city by area — urban core, sprawling suburbs, beaches, and river frontage — and features such as St. Johns River, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve, Intracoastal Waterway, Little Talbot Island keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Atlantic Beach jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: When can the bats in my Neptune Beach attic be excluded?
faqs.a: During Florida's legal exclusion window: August 15 through April 15. From April 16 to August 14, maternity season, excluding or blocking bats is prohibited because flightless pups would be trapped inside. If you call in summer, we inspect, identify the species — evening bats are typical in Neptune Beach homes — seal the openings the colony is not using, and schedule the one-way exclusion for the first legal week. A single bat loose in living space is different: isolate the room and call the same day.

faqs.q: Raccoons keep raiding my Baldwin feed room — what actually works?
faqs.a: Deny the meal and harden the room, in that order. Feed in metal cans with locking lids, no open bags, and the raccoon traffic drops within days; then we trap the committed individuals hanging around and seal the room's eave and door gaps with real hardware cloth, not chicken wire, which raccoons tear. A live-captured raccoon here is released on your land or within Duval County on 40-plus acres with written permission, within 24 hours — but the sealed feed room is what keeps the next one from applying for the job.

Baldwin.wildlife_intro:
Baldwin is Duval's rural western town — a railroad and US-90 crossroads surrounded by timberland, farms, and the county's quietest roads. Properties are bigger, barns and equipment sheds outnumber garages, and the wildlife is country-strong: raccoons in feed storage, opossums and skunks under porches and outbuildings, armadillos and pocket gophers in the fields and yards, and deer — never a removal subject — browsing every garden. The Brandy Branch and McGirts Creek bottoms keep the wet-ground animals close.

Baldwin work is property work: we walk land, not just a house, and rank the fix list — coop security, feed storage, porch skirting, attic sealing — by what protects your animals and buildings first. Snake calls get careful identification out here on the forest fringe, where the venomous list is the full northern set but the daily reality is black racers and ratsnakes keeping the rodent count down around the barns, a service we point out before removing anything.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Mayport?

We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.
